So I was one of the people who tracked this game from pretty much the start. I backed it because I loved the idea of the setting and the Papers, Please-style gameplay. Now that I've finished the final product I can say I got both a little more and a little less then I anticipated.

So let's start with what was good.


From what I saw this game looked like a 1984-style distopian future game. It seemed like you would play as an evil institution with no goal but to moniter what people think. As it turned out, the game made it much more complicated, in a good way, that is.

The final product had a story far more intriguing then what I expected. As it turns our, the DoL (That's Department of Liberty, the department you work for) Does infringe on the privacy of everyone, but it also stops criminals, terrorists and even helps people deal with a natural disaster at one point. On the other hand the system can also be abused. even by yourself if you so desire. Still, there is acctually a bit of an argument for the work you do in this game. I expected it to be very one-sided but the game proved me wrong.

Aside from that, watching your character change over time, getting richter and with that more morally flexible, is also a lot of fun. As you rise trough the ranks of the game the department also pulls more and more power towards it. The change from the current world to an all-monitoring police state doesn't come instantanious, but slowly, as I imagine it would in reality as well. The story took me about 40 hours to complete.

Lastly, on the list of good things are the suspects. Every one of them has a personal profile and getting and image of who they are by reading through their ever-increasing personal information is also a lot of fun. Without giving to much away, you sometimes get to know stuff about suspects that they don't even know themselves.


Now on to the stuff I expected more from.

So the gameplay looked like it would be very fun. You sort through every suspect and decide if they're dangerous or not. Now this is pretty much what you do, and it starts of being a lot of fun, but the gameplay is very slow to add new elements. It takes very long before the game becomes more challanging. Also maybe it's because I played the game quite intensively, but it got a little boring after a while. To me the gameplay started to feel like a chore near the end. I believe they should have made more variety in the missions by adding more stuff. I tended to stop playing the game when the gameplay got too dull for me. Then after a while I'd go back to it for the story.

There is also the fact that there is no timer. You can take as long as you want to finish your mission. I'm personally a little split on this fact. On the one side, I'm glad you can just take your time. I personally get quite stressed when a game gives you a timelimit and I'm pretty sure I'm not the only one on this. I also like that you can just take your time and learn all about a suspect if you like. It gives you a chance to enjoy all the detailed profiles that are in the game.
On the other side I do feel like not having a time limit makes the game a little easy. Mostly at the beginning you can just do most missions flawlessly because there is no limit to how long you can take reading about a suspect.

So if you're looking for a game with a really intriguing story and are willing to put up with getting bored of the gameplay a little from time to time, I would advise getting this game. The story really is great and it totally made the game worth it for me. If you want to buy this game for the gameplay, maybe try playing the Alpha or Beta version first and see if you would like more of that. And when I say more I mean quite a lot more.

[b][i]Need to Know[/i][/b] is a surveillance simulation, the gameplay of which is somewhat reminiscent of the cold and  calculated [i]papers, please[/i]. You assume the role of an employee of an NSA-like organization called The Department of Liberty, and take care of checking people's browsing history and other personal information to identify a possible security risk. The game gives you more options and scary ways to control the longer you play and rise in security clearance. There is always an elementary question floating in the room: Do you stand up for individual rights or do you help to create an uncontrollable police state.

With its topics, [b][i]Need to Know[/i][/b] is not only closer to reality than many other games, it also creates a completely new game approach that will involve many moral decisions. The gameplay, which is basically just scanning data and making quick decisions, is very close to the border crossing simulation [i]papers, please[/i]. Nevertheless, since then hardly any studios have dared to deal with a political issue that affects us all in a similarly dry and fascinating way.

[b]THE GOOD[/b]
- Memorable characters
- Nice story events
- Wonderful atmosphere
- Highly addictive

[b]THE BAD[/b]
- Won't appeal to everyone
- Takes some trial and error 

[h1]8/10[/h1]

DISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY | GOOD | [b][u]GREAT[/u][/b] | AMAZING | MASTERPIECE

EDIT: I changed from not recommended to recommended. Because the game (tactics) change after reaching clearance level 8. Still the below criticizm is applied, but for a game with this pricetag it doesn't to that bad.

So i was hyped for this game from the start & a early kickstarter funder, but it feels like a disappointment for now.
I specially played this game for a few hours to see if it just has a slow start. But sadly it doesn't only have a slow start.. It keeps slow (might even call it boring). 
Only positive note i have at this moment is, that the story is well written and has some noticable real life scenarios.

Another bad thing (in my opinion) is the time it takes to unlock new ablilities. This only happens when you reach a new/higer clearence level. 
I have more then 4 hours into the game. And i only just unlocked clearance level 8 and therby new abilities. This takes to long in my opinion..

The game has the "beta" feel all over itself. Feels cluncky, UI is horrible to work with & windows get blocked constantly. Rules window should be movable at least.
Crashes at weird moments and nothings happening at the same point after restarting the game.

Also the evidence that needs to be collected, can be very conflicting. The rules states that something needs to be collected. But it it isn't directly linked to your suspect but a contact. The game states that you made a wrong choice.

Just as many i was hoping for a "Papers, Please" like gameplay and challenge, but than in a intelligence styled jacket.
This game is disappointing on all fonts:
- Gets boring soon, game also needs some kind of speed mode.
- Sometimes very unclear/conflicting what kind of evidence needs to be collected.
- You get new ways to check on people but no new tools to use, but only whit new clearance levels.
- Just point and click/memory playstyle. I miss some sort of typing involved (for example keyboard shortcuts), playing as an analist.
- Some times theres logic in "linking" people or suspects together early on. You just/simply can't... This is only possible when the game tells you to.
- (to hide spoilers) You do the same thing anywere.
- Buying stuff.. Ehh, whats the use of this? Whats the use of making money in this game anyway. I don't even have to pay rent.. 
- Weird saving structure. Log out before "End Session" aaaand start all over again with the same mission.
- When you "start over" a session by quitting the game. The location and names of the suspects is the same every time & also their logs.
- Crashes mid game (had three in less than 4 hours of gameplay).

It's just constantly doing the same thing.. Over and over.
This is the thing with most games and isn't that big of an issue. 

The issue with this game is, that there isn't enough variation in "what" to do. 
There is just to little to do to keep it interesting. It's way too late in the game & taking way too long to get there, if you even get there you're interest in this game is most likely already gone.

Still putting all the negative points aside. For their first (major) game, it's actually quite good.
I'm certain they will improve the game and crush some bugs in the oncoming days. So lets see how this plays out!

Just finished my first run, at 20 hours, and I can safely say it likely won't be my last.

This games takes the themes present in games like Orwell and Papers, Please and runs with them, in a very satisfying story that had me legitimately questioning myself and my views at times.

The gameplay itself is solid, barring a typo here or there, or a finicky object not recognizing the mouse being over it once or twice. Its really easy to get into, and after at most an hour, its second nature.

All told, an excellent game, made by a shockingly small dev team that deserves much more attention. Here's to future success, Monomyth!

[h1]Decide the fate of citizens of the world in this surveillance thriller![/h1]

You start the game by creating your character. Only gripe I have here is that there aren’t many choices as far as looks goes. It’d be nice to have more than one face type for the male and female. After that, you go through a very detailed tutorial that goes through the basics of what it will take to get you through the job you’ll be tasked with.

The game is deals with a story that’s shaped by your choices as you completed various assignments, gather evidence, flex your powers, and gather profiles. You don’t have to snoop either. As you progress through the game, you’ll have various choices that will allow you to take a stand against the very government organization you work for. A regular in-game cyber revolutionary. 

However, doing more for your boss means a higher clearance level and a higher clearance level means unlocking cooler (albeit creepier) powers, once classified information, lots more money and of course, prestige. With a higher salary, you can impress or intimidate your peers with purchases like new homes and more.

The game play is slow, but goes as fast as you want it to. I mean that in the sense that if you’re the type like me that combs through evidence and meticulously pieces together a person's profile, this will be the game for you. The main story clues are littered throughout your missions. So keep your eyes peeled. 

The music fits the narrative and the UI is clean. The developers are constantly listening and are active on the Steam Discussions. So, if there is a bug you come across, post to the Discussions and you can be sure a developer will take your problem into account. The only bug I came across was the weird save bug where my game would not save, but after a few updates, the saves are working.

I backed the game, but it's $14.99 and runs about 8-10 if you’re not rushing through it. You can definitely stretch that time out by investigating and going through the side content of which there’s a good amount of. The developers have said they plan on adding more content after the game’s ending and that you will be able to continue after your end of game save.

I recommend Need to Know: The Mass Surveillance Thriller Game. If you enjoy intrigue, espionage, and tools at your fingertips for finding out people’s secrets, then this game is for you. It’s a slow burn that works your detective skills and you can be either for or against the government. The game still has a few bugs, but the developers are quickly churning out updates and changelogs that address concerns.

I feel the need to review this now of all times, during the stream of update. Need To Know is fantastic, but it had glaring flaws at launch. I don't believe that this is cause for negative reviews, especially since so many people tend to make a review, and never change it. So here we are.

The game itself is great. Fantastic story, interesting gameplay in the realm of Papers Please/Orwell (Wow bet you've never heard that one before), and compelling decisions, such as the option to weasel your way out of major financial pits by looking at the person who you'd be paying's profile. 

But it was a bit...unclear at first. I spent a lot of time figuring out how to work certain features, as when I first started playing, there had been no updates. No updates, no bug reports, nothing. I was on a 5 hour plane ride, which turned out to be the best time to learn, because I had the time and patience to do it. Once I hit ground, there was already a post about the upcoming stream of updates, bug reports, and immediate fixes and additions to the game to help with clarity.

As of posting this, there have been about 9 updates the help with clarity and bugs. Some may see this as a lack of playtesting. I see it as the devs being incredible accomodating and helpful. You can test a game for months, and still come out with bugs and issues that you didn't foresee because your testers just weren't indicative of EVERYONE playing the game. It happens. And these guys were prepared to handle any complaints. 

From the time I put the game down because of how I was stuck on the first Evidence Wave mission, to the time I picked it back up a day and a half later, major steps were taken to make even that mission in particular less brutally confusing. It's a walk in the park now, and a great introduction to the level style. 

All in all, this is more of a positive review of the devs than a positive review of the game. Because the game is phenomenal, and will continute to get better. The devs just happen to be...well, better than most that I've had to deal with.

I feel the game is quite a bit of fun but some of the negative reviews are correct in pointing out that instructions are sometimes less than clear.

On your first day of "work" (after getting hired) the mission briefing doesn't really explain specifically what you need to do.  I played the alpha and beta of this game and I can tell you that they actually did a better job of explaining this, not sure why they altered it.  Also they changed the assignment "rules" screen which used to be divided between suspicious people and suspicious data, now it just lists everything in a single list.  I personally liked it the old way but that may just be a subjective thing.

For those who are confused here are a few pointers to get you started:

1. On each suspects profile open their evidence which will be their web browsing history and/or their phone records.

2. If you find one of the names or websites in the assignment rules in those sections you need to:
   a) right click and select blacksheep tool
   b) select the relevant data (name or website)
   c) select the rule it relates to in the rules page
   d) mark the suspect as a "Threat" using the lightning (powers) button

3. If you find no evidence matching the rules, just click the powers button and select "Safe".

I don't know why the devs thought it would be a good idea to leave the above (or similar) instructions out of their game as it is bound to put people off, so yeah, I can understand some of the negatives so far.  But personally, I'm marking this as "recommended" because I'm enjoying it and I can say from playing the beta that the story gets more interesting as you get further into it.

Having said that, I really do hope the devs sort out this point of making things clearer to first time users.

I like this game. I would recommend this game, but it needs to change the way that it's marketed. I agree with the top review that does not recommend the game about their frustrations with the game. I think Need to Know markets itself as a game for people who really liked the Orwell games, and offers the same kind of choice paths that it would, when in reality there is a single linear path you can follow in this game because of the inability to pick and choose who you want to work with; the game mechanic forces you to work with everyone who presents themselves.

Like I said, I would recommend this game. I really enjoyed playing it. But I don't like it when games offer choices and branching story paths when really there isn't much deviation offered at all.

Having waited a long time since the Kickstarter ended I was really excited for this game. Then in the first playthrough I failed the Tutorial... which was surprising, I didn't think that was possible to do that. My first game was a mess, particularly due to the scaling of UI and the controls were not very clear. I failed the timed mission and wasn't really getting into the story at all because of frustration. 

Maybe a day or two later update 1.14 came through and it changed everything for the better. I can see everything in the foreground/background, stop the map from spinning the targets out of view and actually focus on the tasks. 
Having reached CL9 things started to actually matter and my character was making the shady deals I'd hoped for from the initial kickstarter description. These choices were a big part of the pull of this game for me. Do I sell Torrent users data to the DoL Agent to buy the Camera Drone, or sell instead to the underground hackers aiming to expose the DoL system? Should I help my sister with her money trouble before she will admit about it to me, what if I don't?

The game is good, better after the first hour definitely. Many people mention Papers, Please and I can see that too. Once you get past CL10 and the missions start to open up a bit it is a much better experience, I'm looking forward to breaking into CL7 very soon.

Also, for now, Monomyth are updating things pretty regularly and making noticable differences to the performance and interface for Need To Know. Its worth a try!

So far, this game looks super promising. I too failed the initiation, but I simply took it again as there is a save point, and read the rules a little more.

The whole interface is nicely done, and the interlinking story is intriguing. The game definitely needs more of a tutorial though, to open with. Having said all that, I'm really excited for the future of this game. It looks like further into the game there are some really original challenges. I've only played a few hours into the game, but I'll revisit it soon and see if I can get to grips with it.

Potentially, an awesome game.

Overall I did like playing the game but I feel it could be way better. I backed the game on Kickstarter and finally took the time to play through it.

I mostly liked the game the game mechanics but it was too long for me with about 25-30h to complete. I felt some clearance levels were stretching for way too long and a shorter experience would have been more enjoyable.

The story is completely linear and you only have an illusion of choice with the dialogue. The only variation possible from the story is to lose. I made the choice to not interact with anyone with the dating app but the story forces you to be in couple with your hometown friend. I never leaked data to Denys but it still ends up backfiring at you. Same thing goes with Tripwire, you have no other way to handle them.

During the game, I never felt there was much at stake. I would have liked to have some dilemma when making a decision for suspects. The only times I wasn't 100% in compliance was because I made slight mistakes, never because I was compelled to protect people or serve some personnal interest. So most of the time I had no interest to know how much % of compliance I gained, nor my ranking changed.

The part I most enjoyed was the end where the rythm was different, even if it was still linear, I liked the sense of story progression and the interrogation gameplay.

I would love to see a sequel, maybe shorter with a non linear story and more stakes.

review_text_raw:
This is not an easy game nor a polished one. I sense the direction of this game was focused towards a giant sandbox of snooping and somewhere along its devcycle someone said, "Hey, this isn't a game." Then someone else said, “Okay, we have all these things the player can do. Read emails, check contacts. Put people on watchlists… How do we make this into a game?” 

The answer of course was to have the player click on links, clicking on the right ones giving  the player points, or if they got it wrong taking points away. But that was too simple, and not very fun, so they added a couple tools to click on the links in different ways and it made it better. And the Devs (who by this point knew exactly how to use each different link clicking tools) said, “Behold! Fun!” And that’s probably as far as playtesting ever got; to the point where the small team of developers had fun playing their own game. 

This is always a problem with small indies with big visions,  they didn’t have time to playtest and get substantitive player feedback. And the biggest problem this game actually has is that the player doesn't receive feedback until  they’ve already failed. Of course, you can review these mistakes after you've failed, but with all the data you need to take in, it is difficult to parse exactly what you did wrong or even how you failed in some cases.

Despite these problems,  this game has there is a good core gameplay loop and a pretty fascinating story. KtK is a competent game in many senses and does not deserved to be tossed aside as a bad game when it is simly missing satisfying feedback.

With time I imagine this game’s player feedback will be fixed. And if it ever is, I would wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone with an interest in "connect the dots" style gameplay and Snowden Era cyberspying.  Right now, the only people I would recommend it to are people who not only love the genre and click on the right thing mechanics, but also have a high tolerance for failing and vigorously studying their failures and don't mind reading forum posts to figure stuff out.

Edit for patches: The developers have accomplished a lot in making the early gameplay more intelligible.

review_text_raw:
I have not finished the game!! This is one of the BEST dystopian simulations i've played. Similar to Orwell, as other reviewers have pointed out, but EVEN BETTER! 

Things I loved:
I love the challenge. It's definitely a game you have to pay attention to and make correct choices. 
There are different facets to the game that allows you to balance home and work life and develop numerous relationships. These are not optional. NPCs will just force you to talk through the phone or at work. 
Relevant story that builds onto itself and you are ultimately working towards the final goal which is to identify and locate Cloud Dweller ( i believe thats his alias) 
I like the characters. I like the story. It's very well written and done. And I love that I can be sassy with that dude at work that everyone hates. LOL 
It's a long and complex game. It was longer and has more content than I expected.
The dating app KILLS ME! Those profiles XD no wonder people are single.

Things I hated:
Some choices lead directly into game over. I ended the game multiple times unintentionally with no warning through dialogue selection. Like I was talking to the reporter/boyfriend/friend? Not sure of his purpose yet. Anyway, I accidentally said I worked at DoL and BAM! game over. Thankfully the autosave system allows you to log back in and pick up before you make that choice. But it was just so sudden and happened multiple times during different scenarios.
Everyone forces you to work for them. You have to keep selling secrets to keep your reputation up with everyone so they don't either blackmail you or fire you. It's annoying. I would rather have more choices. I don't like being two-faced and this game forces you to be that.

Overall - I still recommend it. I keep wanting to finish it and it has held my interest which few games do. However, I doubt I'll replay it. Either way - it's definitely worth the price! Buy it on sale if you can, but even $15 is still decent for this game.

KEEP UP THE GOOD WORK!

review_text_raw: I got this game because I really loved Orwell and found it to be a thought provoking and thrilling story experience. This game, although comparable in premise, is definitely unique in its gameplay and purpose--you get prompted to "participate" (I say this loosely because your dialogue options are limited) in text/phone conversations as well as chats with your coworkers, and you can do "off the record" work from home. Like Papers, Please, more surveillance options open up as you play and there is an underlying plot. But I do have some issues with the mechanics of the game; as I mentioned before, dialogue options are very limited, and you're required to pursue certain paths in the story (you can't chose *not* to work for specific groups. You have to take all opportunities or you get a game over, which is kind of annoying). There's also some bugs and small annoying "Features"... The instructions/tutorials/exposition text all automatically progress (no "click to continue") so you can easily miss out on instructions or text. Sometimes the tutorial messages will get stuck and stop proceeding even though you've done what they've asked. Then it won't continue until you've gone ahead and figured out the tutorial section on your own. The game could use some more polish, but isn't unplayable and is fun enough.

This game takes inspirations from Orwell and Papers, Please. Any fan of either will like Need To Know. It had a great story, and each "work day" comes with a new set of objectives and challenges, as you delve deeper into the shadowy underworkings of government surveillance. The story was pretty much on rails the whole time, though there were options to deviate, which I didn't explore on my first playthrough. You can expect 15-20 hours to finish the game. I got it on a sale, but even at full price, 15 bucks for 15+ hours seems like a good trade-off to me.

Give it a go, you won't be disappointed.

Nonetheless, the game falls rather short considering there really are no choices you can make (technically, there are, but these choices just mean the game is over before its real ending). I value choices in these types of games more than anything, however the developers really had just one type of character in mind; you can't be completely devoted to the Department, and you can't be a rebel either. Also, although day-to-day duties are interesting at first, later they become really boring, except for few meaningful investigations, so the developers could have made the game shorter without sacrificing anything, really. Still recommended for people who like these types of games, just don't expect too much.

The story is fairly well written. It can be a little iffy at times when it comes to the grand scheme of things, but if you hold your suspension of disbelief, mainly the idea that someone could rise through the ranks like that and that you are pretty much the lynchpin for everything that happens in the story, it works well. I do wish that there were more outs from the story as time goes by, but you can only put so many options into a game before you start over-writing it. 
While I'm talking about endings, I'll bring up probably my least favorite one. One of the final endings is just one or two sentences and then it boots you back to the main menu. I get that they weren't trying to take a side in the underlying debate in the game, but it does seem a little strange when you have dialogue choices mean almost the exact same thing multiple times in the story.
I love how the characters are implemented into the story. On Day 2 meet someone who has your back. And that same person is with you until the final major decision. He's well developed and seems almost human with the way he's written, having real motivations behind his actions that are very relatable to many people. Almost every main character you interact with has an effect on the story if they don't straight up give you a way out of the story. For those that don't give you a way out, they still plant seeds into your mind. What those seeds may be will vary and what they grow into is up to you, but the fact still remains that they have really thought the writing out.
The mechanics of the game have also been very thought out. It may look like dots on a map when you first start out, but it quickly expands when you hover over that dot. As you go through their data, it plants more seeds of doubt in the system. And then you have to click one of two buttons. Do they go free, or do they not go free? No matter what button you click, there will be text that pops up. That text tells you what happens to that person. Solely because of what you decided to do. The weight behind all that is monumental at times. It makes you question your decisions at times. And it is absolutely well done.
The commentary on the security/liberty debate is where this game really shines. By establishing a connection with someone who will be on your side until the end of the game, it ensures that the line for most people will be blurred. It's story is written well enough to have it come out to you at points and ask you if what you are doing is right and warns you that it's a dangerous path that lies ahead if you continue down it. Can't go into too much detail without spoiling a lot of the game. If you don't care about spoilers, go back up and reread the section that I start by mentioning the commentary.

It's fun.

review_text_raw:
[b] Premise [/b]
You are a government employee working for the 'Department of Liberty' where your job is to spy on/profile suspects and targets. You 'match' pertinent information (dating profile, purchases, social media posts) to mission based criteria. 

[b] Play it if you like.... [/b]
If you played and enjoyed 'Papers, Please',  or 'Orwell' then chances are you'll like this game. If you like the concepts of 1984, V for Vendetta then you'll enjoy the story. And if you really just like sorting and matching information like a nerd (like me) then you'll love the gameplay

[b] Pros [/b]
Great gameplay concept and the profiling aspects are really interesting - a lot of thought has been put into these elements and I enjoyed seeing what I'd get access to next.
Progression through the 'ranks' is done at a decent pace which keeps things fresh. Theres also some evening missions to supplement your income
Theres also a nice mix of mission types - I enjoyed the 'waves' missions where you are given more information each 'wave' in order to keep or eliminate a suspect. 
Plenty of moral ambiguity to the main characters - although some are cartoonish. 
Overall story is quite compelling and I was always eager to see how it would progress (I did a lot of 'Oh I'll just play one more mission before I switch off.....')
Again, if you're an information-sorting nerd like me you'll just love the gameplay.

[b] Cons [/b]
UI is a bit painful sometimes - you can't zoom into information (you can change the UI to either 'IN YOUR FACE' or 'far away' but neither is a good compromise). For example when I had to look at a persons job on their social network it was so tiny I could barely make it out. And again when selecting suspects from a clustered area I couldn't highlight the right profile. I think this could be improved by making better use of the screen...there is SO MUCH empty space! I like to have the mission rules up all the time to match to but I constantly have to scroll through them at the bottom of the screen even though there was a huge empty space to the left of the screen totally un-used.
Story con - like a lot of these games you're given the illusion of freedom of choice. 

[b] Overall [/b]
I played the game through in 25 hours and was fully addicted to it as I was playing it. I think it just avoided getting stale mainly because the main story always kicked in at the right moments. If the UI could be sorted I'd have been so much happier.

review_text_raw:
A surprisingly fun gem of a title that... if it wants to or not, teaches the players that the world is complex.

Unlike Papers Please, where if you make a mistake, you can see plain as day what you did wrong and how you can improve, Need to Know is as grey as it's central themes. There are going to be choices you have to make with incomplete information. You might flag evidence that game rejects, or ignore evidence the game was expecting you to flag- and you might do so fully believing your choice was right. There is an margin of subjectivity in this game that is wonderfully refreshing. You're not going to have all the information and you have to make choices. 

For many players this might be frustrating, fully believing you made a choice and the game just disagreed with you. But that's life. Rarely does that wrong choice fully lead to a game over and the plot itself is good enough to keep me invested. 

My biggest surprises is that this title isn't more well known. It's a solid game.

review_text_raw:
[h1]What is this game?[/h1]
It is the foremost NSA-watch-the-world-from-an-office simulator you will find as of the time of writing this review, and possibly for a long time.

You play a young man, joining a government agency. The rabbithole goes deep, and you are thrusted into a position of Orwellian surveillance, intrigue and thrill.

Starting at the bottom, you analyze simple things. Metadata, browser history and try to piece together a puzzle that is very clearly Need To Know. Given only slight glimpses of what is truly going on in this world. As you progress, you will advance in rank, getting a higher and higher level of clearance, and quickly find yourself face to face with the choice of whether or not to use your access for the good of the agency, the government, the country. the people or even yourself. 

Utilizing your powers of cyber-espionage to predict and even outright uncover your flings interests and hobbies, getting the IRS to get off your back, finding your sister/brother during an emergency or even getting out of paying your rent.

It very quickly becomes apparent what kind of power it actually is you are trusted with, and you will immediately realize why exactly it is so dangerous if left unchecked.

Don't just take it from me. Take it from the very person who knows this the best when he retweeted the game
[i]"Art imitates life."
~Edward Snowden[/i]

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The graphic artstyle of this game is great. It's minimalistic, but still detailed in the way it is done. The whole layout gives a sense of a point-and-click adventure, and for all intents and purposes it is.

Graphically, this game is unique in the way it focuses on the mechanics and uses the art direction to enhance them. You're never distracted by what's on the screen or in your peripheral vision, yet even after many hours (I'm writing this after a 24 hour bender on this game) it never ceases to be interesting or captivating. Artistically, it's very clear it was drawn by somebody who is passionate about the game, and it shows.

[h1]Gameplay & Mechanics[/h1]
The game had a very rough start at launch, with virtually no tutorial. That has been corrected. The team behind this game are very active both on the games own Subreddit, taking into account all the reports being thrown at them and have now rolled out the fourth daily patch in a row. Where else do you see that?

The gameplay itself is good. However, I will be the first to admit that it can be un-intuitive. They have and still are taking steps to improve on this, but the game itself doesn't suffer that heavily under the previous or current issues. It plays like one would very much expect of a game of this type, yet it manages to do [i]so much[/i] with the established fundamentals of the game. Despite having pre-ordered this the moment I saw it almost half a year ago (it has been in development since 2016 and undergone many redesigns), I was honestly afraid that it would end up like most games of this caliber do, where you end up feeling the developers grasping at straws, and the game for its breath as it tries to reskin the same old mechanics and play them off as changes to the gameplay. The gameplay [b]does not change[/b], and thats strangely enough the charm and appeal.

Connect the dots as you chain together events from mere fragments of information such as e-mails, texts, social media, phone calls, browser history, bank account transcripts and decide the fate of the very people you've been spying on from behind your screen. Will you label them a threat for speaking their mind in, what they assumed to be total privacy and confidence, or will you stand up and become a whistleblower and help bring down this omniscient, omnipotent government entity?

You do unlock new abilities progressively as you pass through the ranks of this fictional quasi-NSA government agency, but they do not change the way the game plays, only improve and enhance upon it. All too often do you see games desperately trying to change its own formula throughout the span of the game, and it more often than not ends up sweeping the rug out from under themselves. You won't find that here.

I have never been much for point-and-click games. So much so that I own none except for Orwell and Need to Know. If you have played Orwell, you will without a doubt find yourself enamored with this title.

On a final note, I'll add that there is a story. Getting into it here wouldn't do it justice, and I haven't even completed the game yet. But it will draw you in. Seemingly unrelated events tie together into something larger, and as you scale the ranks of this clandestine government, denying counter-surveillance groups information (or perhaps supplying it yourself), so does the plot thicken and grow.

I would most definitely recommend this game to pretty much anybody who likes a captivating experience.

It is not without flaws, but the developers have rolled out daily fixes since release, and are obviously very passionate about this game. It's not early access, but it isn't a triple-A polished and buffed product, either. But it is getting there.

Take it from the very person who knows this the best when he retweeted the game [i]"Art imitates life." ~Edward Snowden[/i] [h1]Visuals[/h1] The graphic artstyle of this game is great. It's minimalistic, but still detailed in the way it is done. The whole layout gives a sense of a point-and-click adventure, and for all intents and purposes it is. Graphically, this game is unique in the way it focuses on the mechanics and uses the art direction to enhance them. You're never distracted by what's on the screen or in your peripheral vision, yet even after many hours (I'm writing this after a 24 hour bender on this game) it never ceases to be interesting or captivating. Artistically, it's very clear it was drawn by somebody who is passionate about the game, and it shows. [h1]Gameplay & Mechanics[/h1] The game had a very rough start at launch, with virtually no tutorial. That has been corrected. The team behind this game are very active both on the games own Subreddit, taking into account all the reports being thrown at them and have now rolled out the fourth daily patch in a row. Where else do you see that? The gameplay itself is good. However, I will be the first to admit that it can be un-intuitive. They have and still are taking steps to improve on this, but the game itself doesn't suffer that heavily under the previous or current issues. It plays like one would very much expect of a game of this type, yet it manages to do [i]so much[/i] with the established fundamentals of the game. Despite having pre-ordered this the moment I saw it almost half a year ago (it has been in development since 2016 and undergone many redesigns), I was honestly afraid that it would end up like most games of this caliber do, where you end up feeling the developers grasping at straws, and the game for its breath as it tries to reskin the same old mechanics and play them off as changes to the gameplay. The gameplay [b]does not change[/b], and thats strangely enough the charm and appeal. Connect the dots as you chain together events from mere fragments of information such as e-mails, texts, social media, phone calls, browser history, bank account transcripts and decide the fate of the very people you've been spying on from behind your screen. Will you label them a threat for speaking their mind in, what they assumed to be total privacy and confidence, or will you stand up and become a whistleblower and help bring down this omniscient, omnipotent government entity? You do unlock new abilities progressively as you pass through the ranks of this fictional quasi-NSA government agency, but they do not change the way the game plays, only improve and enhance upon it. All too often do you see games desperately trying to change its own formula throughout the span of the game, and it more often than not ends up sweeping the rug out from under themselves. You won't find that here. I have never been much for point-and-click games. So much so that I own none except for Orwell and Need to Know. If you have played Orwell, you will without a doubt find yourself enamored with this title. On a final note, I'll add that there is a story. Getting into it here wouldn't do it justice, and I haven't even completed the game yet. But it will draw you in. Seemingly unrelated events tie together into something larger, and as you scale the ranks of this clandestine government, denying counter-surveillance groups information (or perhaps supplying it yourself), so does the plot thicken and grow. I would most definitely recommend this game to pretty much anybody who likes a captivating experience. It is not without flaws, but the developers have rolled out daily fixes since release, and are obviously very passionate about this game. It's not early access, but it isn't a triple-A polished and buffed product, either. But it is getting there.

In a nutshell: A good game, with some great ideas, that needs some polish on the execution, with a number of technical and interface issues that drag down a good story and a great idea.

Put simply, the idea of a game where you move through the hierarchy of a sinister spying agency is a great one, and this game's greatest success so far in my time with it has been not only showing how quickly the power to snoop on everything and everyone can go wrong, but also, and crucially, how it can still also be a force for good. The story is I think the strongest point of the game for me, because it's depiction of the ironically named 'Department of Liberty' is not really as some cartoon villain 'Illuminati conspiracy' but as a government organisation set up in response to a great crisis which, at least initially, is comprised largely of ordinary people. Sure, some of the people you meet in the game are dubiously motivated at best, but the game reinforces in the narrative consistently that there are good people in the DoL, who genuinely believe the spying they engage in is justified and indeed, there are examples in game where the power you use does make a real difference.

I can't say much more without spoiling the hell out of the game, but suffice it to say, if story is what you want, the game offers an intriguing story, and while it may not be a Tom Clancy tale, I've found it engaging and compelling.

Likewise, the gameplay offers good challenge, requiring you to carefully dissect the data you sift through, looking not just for keywords early on but as time goes on, looking for more complicated and easily missed details, like tracing suspicious bank activity with logs of suspicious contacts, and working out if they match up or are a red herring. These shifting challenges do a reasonably good job of building on each other, with each clearance level you go through iterating on previous challenges with an extra layer of complexity, and this organic growth of difficulty is largely well-executed. But it does lead into the big problem in the game: communication.

This game has a real problem communicating with the player, and I think it's largely down to an interface that can be clunky and unintuitive. Partially this is down to bugs, like notifications on your phone not displaying so you're left staring blankly waiting for something to happen, to more egregious errors like typos in the keywords you're looking for, and contextual menus being hard to close once opened and obscuring the screen. These are all fixable issues thankfully, and while irritating, they don't for me drag the game down too much, but the sooner they are resolved, the better, and they are likely to irritate some players too much to continue.

Also, the game can be ambiguous in what the objectives of each day actually require. For instance, you might be asked to look for keywords, but the game isn't good at indicating whether you need a literal, case-sensitive match of the word, or a contextual match. For instance, if the keyword was 'Bomb Kit' and you saw a log that said 'making my own bombs in a kit', you might well flag that as suspicious, and logically, it totally is, but because the game is looking for a case-sensitive, exact match, it marks you down as wrong for it. Again, these issues are not exactly common, but they're infrequent enough to annoy, and for me are the biggest issue of all in the game, but again, can be fixed by the devs.

So in the end, I recommend this game, but I do it with an advisory: if you want a good story, with fun challenges and an engaging concept of government intelligence and the morality of that, then I highly recommend it, but make sure you go in right now knowing there are currently technical and design issues, and while these will likely be fixed, as of the time of this review they exist, and they can annoy. Hopefully you'll be like me, and able to see through the roughness to the diamond within, and enjoy the experience for what it is, not what you necessarily would like it to be.

I do recommend this game but it’s not without its faults and some of those are gameplay problems.  I would give this a 3/5 if such a ratings system existed on Steam.

This game reminds me a lot of Papers, Please but it lacks the urgency of PP.  There is a clock ticking down but as far as I could tell there were no repercussions to letting it run out.  Most of the missions were solved within 2 hours of the clock ticking and there’s no pro or con to finishing by a certain time.  This is one of many parts of the game where I thought, “Why is this here, it serves no purpose”.

The after work missions get extremely tedious.  I did all of them but I wonder if you didn’t whether the ending would have been different.  Something tells me it would not have mattered.  You get money but besides one particular time, it doesn’t matter if you do anything with it or not.  There’s another after work “task” that you can do that does nothing other than add a distraction (trying to be vague to be spoiler free here) and I stopped doing it halfway through the game with again, no repercussions.

Trying to select points on the map is a huge pain especially when there are multiple suspects in a location.  The map keeps scrolling and the location point doesn’t lock very well onto the mouse.  A lot (all maybe?) of the dialogue screens are off-center and near the bottom of the screen.  So you’re watching a cut scene and it’s in the bottom 30% of your computer monitor and not centered. Seems like a weird style choice along with half-hiding the graphics for home/office/etc.  There are a couple of missions that I had to write down data or take pictures of the screen to correlate data between people because there wasn’t a good way of doing this in game.  Also had some graphics issues where the screen would bounce around randomly.

The last act of the game really tried my patience.  I had to restart multiple levels because the data I was pulling wasn’t right and this is already a very lengthy game where there isn’t a meaningful change in mechanics so it was feeling REALLY tedious by this point.

All that having been said, I did enjoy the game from a storyline standpoint and the data correlation/searching aspect.  If there was a sequel with the gameplay problems fixed and the stakes were higher, I would definitely check it out.

Backed it on Kickstarter (I'm even in the credits if you looked!), played it, abandoned it for a few years, and then finally finished it, doesn't mean it's a boring game, hear me out.

Need to Know came from the era of Orwell - which I've also played, loved and reviewed - basically pattern matching gameplay laid on top of a "visual" novel (only without boobs). The gameplay, while has to be involved and brain-teasing, needs to tells a story.

Orwell excelled with being a more aggressively ramped-up authoritarian nightmare. A seemingly more far-fetched future. A story where an outsider can help control information, narratives, and through that, the truth and history.

(Mild spoilers ahead, skip next paragraph if you don't wanna know anything)

Need to Know, on the other hand, writes a story in a near future - where we may be right now, or in a few years. You play as a US citizen, whose sole power is to prosecute, to "just follow orders", and meanwhile trying to survive a personal political hell. You play yourself into becoming a regular crimer, a warcrimer, and a national terrorist. You see repercussion of your own actions in the story. You may justify yourself into believing you're fighting for "the truth"; yet the information you are given keeps getting worse, and it makes you wonder if you're becoming a eugenicist and a fascist. At that point, the only winning move may just be not to play, or yeet yourself into prison.

(Spoiler over)

If you choose to play on, the gameplay is more involved than Orwell - while Orwell only makes you marks single pieces of evidence, Need to Know makes you show the link between different pieces of seemingly unrelated information - only becoming related because you are given inside knowledge of what they may have been doing. Messages, tweets, locations, bank statements, satellite images, heartbeats - all the data we give willingly these days - can and will be used against them. You request more data, you use that data to find incriminating evidence, and you string them together to prosecute them. Everyday is like a mini-Sherlock Holmes mind palace minigame, only it keeps getting more complicated. It can get repetitive, but being engaged to the story and the new data types will help mitigate it a little bit.

The game represents a possible future, and you are a judge, jury, and executioner. Have fun doing war crimes.

Okay, so here we go. I've reached up to CL 3 now and have played the alpha version of this game as well. It's quite a bit of fun and I'm enjoying it.  PLEASE TRY THIS GAME. THE GRIND PAYS OFF.

Pros:
Neat concept, reasonably well executed by what I understand is a fairly novice indy team.
Developers are fixing the bugs
The art style is neat  (was kind of getting tired of Indy game meaning pixelart)
The CODEX facts are kinda funny sometimes and the little easteregg info bits are a nice touch.
The story is reasonably engaging
Fun sort of puzzle-type game
Doesn't feel like papers please
Hope to see new stuff get added in future as Devs are being fairly responsive to community input
The UI is well-optimized (especially when compared to the Beta)
Soundtrack isn't bad either.
The characters do actually feel like real people.
Cons

Sometimes the rules aren't always super clear and this can lead to some serious mission screwups (however, fret not, even if you get a huge compliance ding you can either A) exit the mission before going home (this will restart it from the login screen or B) Just eat the compliance hit because usually the next mission is more forgiving it's usually a couple easy missions then a kind of tough one and then a few easier ones)

The missions can feel a little grind-y. 

There's some stuff missing that seems like it should be there (There's no stock trading system as promised, the shop only has a handfull of items to buy, no cars or anything like what was in the original trailer for this game).

The first couple CLs are a grind. I've got almost 17 hours into the game and I'm at CL 3 (you start at 10). The real fun doesn't really start until about CL 6 or so and I think that's pushing a couple people away from the game.

The Data selling thing is just kind of super annoying and stretches the gameplay out unnecessarily while adding little to the story.

Wish there were more character customization options. 


TL;DR: Neat indy game, responsive development team. Can be a little grind-y through the first bit but gets pretty good after that.

Very fun game that does an excellent job of portraying the slippery slope when dealing with the question of rights vs security.

*** Spoilers ***
You start off with basic tasks like hunting down murderers or catching terrorists, but then a hurricane hits...

... And you're not permitted to go snooping through people's offline data, but you break the law anyway because if you can track them down, you can send FEMA their location and save some lives! So it's fine, right? Sure, some people lose a bit of privacy, but you're rescuing them from the hurricane!

And then as you rise through the ranks you get a bit more power and you start dealing with tracking down serial killers or stopping an active shooter... But then a senator doesn't like the fact that your department is ignoring people's rights to privacy and wants to shut you down...

... So you blackmail her by digging through her data and finding embarassing information to damage her career. Can't have her foolish ideals stand in the way, obstructing your quest to save lives, right?

And then a bunch of corporations give you access to their data, making your job to track down terrorists even easier, and helping you along the way in your original mission to find a man who caused a few nuclear reactors to overload in a massive terrorist attack, but they want a couple favours...

... So you start doing a bit of corporate espionage on the side, but it's fine, I'm sure, because the backroom deals are how you make progress, and no one *really* needs to keep their shopping history private, do they?

But then some of this stuff gets leaked and more politicians start rallying against it. Fools. They don't know how hard you're working to keep this country safe! They don't know how necessary it is to use this data...

... So you launch a disinformation campaign to silence them and ruin their credibility. It was their fault anyways. They threatened the department, and you needed to protect it! You're the only one standing in the way of the terrorists attacking america, so getting your hands dirty sometimes is fine if it's to protect the greater good, right?

So throughout the game you're doing these underhanded deals, blackmail and character assassinations, but it's fine because you're catching terrorists, saving lives, and generally making sure the citizens can go on with their happy little lives. Soon it pays off! You catch a terrorist who leads you to a terrorist who leads you to a whole network of them! ... but they're scattered across the globe, and many of the countries aren't too keen on sending them to the states for judgement...

... Well they stand in your way! They're harbouring enemies of the state, that's basically an act of war, right? You need to show these governments the errors of their ways... Or maybe you can't. Maybe you should arm some of the militant groups in the countries who are more friendly towards US interests... So you start distributing arms to them and help them seize power, but it's fine, right? You toppled a government and installed a few dictatorships, but you've got to help your country! They were basically asking for it anyways by hiding your enemies, right? So what if a few thousand people on the otherside of the world got killed, you're supposed to protect Americans and that's what you're going to do!

But now your powers are growing and word of your department's actions are reaching the journalists, who are writing scathing criticisms of you and turning the people against you... Well you can't have that happen, so you need to silence them, either by getting them fired or threatening them to keep quiet! Freedom of speech is just getting in the way here, this sacrifice is for the good of the nation, right? Right?!

Despite your best efforts public opinion is still slowly turning against you, and the politicians are noticing... well there's an election coming up, so you've got to make sure a politician friendly to your department gets in. Can't have the president disband the department of liberty, there's still so much work left to do! 

... So you blackmail politicians, leak incriminating documents, and funnel support towards your prefered candidate, ensuring she wins the election. You've subverted democracy but it's fine, right? You need to protect the department because it protects the nation! You're the hero of this story after all! You can't let people who don't understand get in the way, right guys? Right?! Sacrifices must be made! It's for the good of the nation! The good of us all! There's no way I could be the villain, right?! I am the hero here!!!!

But of course, it doesn't stop there. You need more power. Even when you're launching military assaults on embassies in foreign nations, even when you drone-strike your own citizens, even when you assassinate the leaders of other countries who once tried to help you but now stand in your way... 

And then you see it. You get betrayed. People want the power your department has, and your boss and other corporations are vying for the systems that now control the world. What was a perfect, all-seeing system is being used as a pawn by people for petty power plays and revenge... to further their own ideals at the expense of everyone else. You know that you need to end this. You need to stop it. The people at the top need to be brought down. A system this powerful can't remain in the hands of those who would abuse it. A system this perfect either needs to be destroyed or to remain under the control of someone who would use it for good... someone like you... And after all, you're the hero, so why not take it? It's for the good of the nation after all... 

*** End Spoilers ***

Unfortunately there's still a few problems with the game. The interface is not nearly as responsive as it should be for as simple a game as this is. Additionally when you get assignments cross-referencing between multiple suspects,... ugh... the limitations of the UI really make themselves known, and despite there being hundreds of HCI papers out there for how to build proper interfaces when comparing data, this game chooses to use none of them. As someone who worked in an Info-vis lab for a while, I can safely say that the method they chose to link data between two different suspects is one of the most annoying and tedious ways they could have possibly done it. You will audiably groan when you see the mission rules "Link evidence when two suspects travel to the same city at the same time.". It is that bad. Fortunately these missions are few and far between, so you don't have to deal with it too often.

I also didn't like that your actions basically had no lasting effects. Any big choice either ends the game or lets you continue playing. I was really hoping that...

*** Spoilers ***
When you get betrayed, you would have a chance to work with the Snow Owl black-ops division instead of with Tripwire to work your way back up to the top. Maybe based on which faction you had a higher reputation with. They're black-ops anyways, with everything they do being classified and deniable, so helping you wouldn't be completely out of the question.
*** End Spoilers ***

That aside, the game was very fun and very satisfying to play. It played around with a lot of neat ideas, and again, I really liked the story. I also liked how it showed your progression from living in a trashy apartment and working in basically a basement closet to living in a super upscale neighbourhood and leading your own division as you progress through the ranks. I highly recommend it.

8/10
